description: This is the official Citadel Solutions LLC team.
summary:
Fire managers need to know whether this season is unusual. But NASA’s 24-year satellite fire record is split between two sensors that can’t be compared directly. MODIS, observing since 2000, is nearing retirement. VIIRS, its successor, detects roughly four times as many hotspots for the same burning, so simply joining the records creates a false surge in fire activity starting in 2012.

We developed a validated harmonization method and a web application built on it. Using the years both sensors overlapped, we derived month-specific conversion factors that place the full record on one consistent, VIIRS-equivalent scale. Tested on 2020–2026 data the model never saw, it achieved +-8.1% error, compared with 78% without harmonization. Our pipeline also detects VIIRS outages, such as during the 2024 Park Fire, and fills them using MODIS data, so major fire events aren’t undercounted.

Users select any area and date range and get a burning activity calendar: a heatmap with accessible color ramps showing monthly activity, comparisons with historical medians, yearly totals and downloadable CSV analytics. Our California pilot covers 1.2 million detections from 2003 to the present, and the pipeline scales to any region.
details:
What it does

The Burning Activity Calendar turns more than two decades of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into one consistent record. Users draw a rectangle on a map or type coordinates, choose a date range, and see a calendar heatmap: one row per year, one square per month, from 2003 to the present. A second view shows each month as a percentage above or below what’s normal for that time of year. Users can click any month to see its uncertainty range, the raw counts from each sensor and data-quality notes, and can download monthly analytics or raw hotspot detections as CSV.

How it works

MODIS (2000–present) and VIIRS (2012–present) can’t be compared directly: VIIRS detects about 4.4 times as many hotspots as MODIS for the same fires. We calculated a conversion factor for each calendar month from the years both sensors were running (2012–2019), then converted MODIS counts to VIIRS-equivalent units, so the 2012 transition shows no artificial jump. We tested the method on 2020–2026, years it never saw: error dropped from 78% without harmonization to 8.1%. We also found days when the VIIRS satellite recorded nothing while MODIS still saw fires. One example is the start of the 2024 Park Fire. We detect these outage days automatically and fill them using converted MODIS data. “Normal” is the median for each calendar month over a fixed 2003–2022 baseline, so comparisons stay consistent.

Benefits and intended impact

Emergency managers, scientists and land managers get a long, consistent fire history for any area, instead of two records that disagree. The calendar answers practical questions quickly: which months usually burn most, which years were worst, and whether this month is unusual. As MODIS retires, our method keeps more than 20 years of history usable alongside VIIRS going forward.

Tools and technologies

  • Data and science: Python, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, matplotlib
  • Backend: FastAPI, served with Uvicorn and managed with uv
  • Frontend: Vue 3, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite, Leaflet with Leaflet-Geoman for map drawing, and OpenStreetMap tiles
  • Deployment: Docker, Google Cloud Run, and GitHub Actions running 31 automated end-to-end checks on synthetic test data
  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m Suomi NPP active fire data, about 1.4 million detections for California
  • AI assistance: Claude, for planning, code review and parts of the code. The team reviewed all of it.

What makes it creative

  • Instead of trusting the satellite record, we checked it. The automatic outage detection catches missing data that would otherwise make one of California’s largest fires look like an ordinary month.
  • Every converted number carries its own uncertainty range and quality flag, so users can see how much to trust each value.
  • Each calendar square shows its number, not just a color, so the data can be read without relying on color perception.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity: testing on years the method never saw, and reporting the error honestly
  • Data quality: VIIRS outages, MODIS gaps and unfinished months are flagged instead of hidden
  • Accessibility: colorblind-safe palettes (Cividis and ColorBrewer PuOr), full keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, and a coordinate form as an alternative to drawing on the map
  • Honest scope: a California pilot, with clear warnings when statewide factors are applied to small areas
  • Reliability: synthetic test data, automated checks, and a single-container deployment that keeps the live demo simple and stable
